paras: The expulsion of Black workers from Coatesville, Pennsylvania, was a series of police roundups in early 1919 in which a constable, local police and the state constabulary drove unemployed Black steel workers out of the town. The NAACP protested to federal and state officials, and the Department of Labor ordered an investigation. Black newspapers presented it as the treatment of war workers whose labor was no longer needed.

Black workers had been recruited in the South and brought to Coatesville in large numbers while its steel plants ran on war orders. After the armistice the mills cut production, and Black residents said hundreds had been discharged from the Midvale plants, leaving some without work or money to leave. Police said crime had risen, and the authorities had begun lining up men who sought free lodging at city hall and ordering them out of town each morning.

The first organized drive took place on a Tuesday, according to a report printed in the Phoenix Tribune on March 15, which does not give the date. Under Constable A. S. Jackson and state police, more than fifty men were rounded up on South First avenue, where Black men gathered in poolrooms and cigar stores. Men who could not produce an employer's check were put into what officers called the "southbound gang," and about thirty were escorted by foot police and mounted constabulary to the Cain bridge south of town and driven out.

Police told the men to "head south and stay away" and announced further raids on all men who could not show residence or employment. The Chicago Defender's correspondent, Charles T. Magill, described raids on the places where Black residents lived and people driven "like cattle" to a point south of the town.

NAACP secretary John R. Shillady telegraphed Secretary of Labor William B. Wilson that discharged Black workmen were allegedly being deported by the state constabulary, protesting their "arrest and deportation." Similar telegrams went to Governor William C. Sproul and the mayor, and the association asked Midvale vice-president William B. Dickson to insure humane treatment of the men.
In late March the Department of Labor ordered an inquiry by Charles J. Fury, a commissioner of conciliation. No report of its findings, or of any action against the officers, appears in the coverage.

The fullest account, in the Phoenix Tribune on March 15, relayed the police explanation of rising crime at length alongside Black residents' account of layoffs. A comment on the same page condemned "herding Negroes like cattle" with no charge of crime and recalled an earlier lynching at Coatesville.

The NAACP release ran with the telegram in the Washington Bee under the headline "No Further Use for Them," in the Omaha Monitor, and in shorter form in the Wisconsin Weekly Blade. The Labor Department brief appeared in the St. Louis Argus, the Cleveland Advocate and, through the Associated Negro Press, the Dallas Express.

The Defender's April 5 report, headed "Whites 'Round Up' Those Who Made War Munitions," was the most condemnatory, calling the drive a plan by southerners to force Black workers back south. In June the Omaha Monitor reprinted a Columbia, South Carolina, editorial that grouped Coatesville with East St. Louis and Springfield as places that used Black labor and would "dump them on the South."

The Phoenix Tribune described men sorted on the street by employment checks, while the Defender said women and children were reportedly among those driven out. The timing is uncertain, since the NAACP telegram printed by the Washington Bee is dated March 4 and already describes deportations. Only the Defender said the drive brought "death to some," without particulars.

reader.title: Expulsion of Black workers from Coatesville, Pennsylvania
bases: Constable, local police and mounted state constabulary rounded up Black men without employment checks and drove them out of town, with more drives announced (A3, A4, A12).

The detailed roundup account (A3, A4) is matched by the NAACP's independent telegram alleging deportation by the state constabulary (A7), the Labor Department's ordered inquiry (A8, A9) and the Defender correspondent's report (A12).

accounts.label: Police account (via Phoenix Tribune report)
accounts.gist: Police said crime had risen since the armistice as idle men loafed and sought free lodging, so they lined men up and ordered them out and would raid and drive out all men who could not show residence or work.

accounts.label: Black residents (via Phoenix Tribune report)
accounts.gist: Black men in Coatesville said Lukens laid off few men but hundreds were discharged from the Midvale plants, and some had no work and no funds to leave.

accounts.label: NAACP
accounts.gist: Discharged Black war workers were allegedly being arrested and deported by the state constabulary; the association demanded federal attention.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Chicago Defender)
accounts.gist: Constable, police and mounted constabulary raided Black residences and drove people, reportedly including women and children, like cattle south of town, in a plan by southerners to force workers back south; the drive brought 'death to some'.

framing.detail: Phoenix Tribune comment: '100 per cent American city herding Negroes like cattle' with no charge of crime, linked to an earlier Coatesville lynching.

Washington Bee headline 'No Further Use for Them' over the NAACP protest.
Chicago Defender: 'Whites Round Up Those Who Made War Munitions', a town with 'an atmosphere of the south'.
Labor Department inquiry run as a plain news brief.
